question.text:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given below. What is $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}?$

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -8 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
Given the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -8 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -22 \\ 21 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

The change-of-coordinates matrix from the basis $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2, \mathbf{b}_3 \}$ to the basis $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2,\mathbf{c}_3 \}$ is given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} = 5\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2- \mathbf{b}_3.$
question.explanation:
First, notice that since $\mathbf{x} =5\mathbf{b}_1+\mathbf{b}_2- \mathbf{b}_3,$ we have

\[ [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Given the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{B}$ and the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C},$ we find the coordinates of $\mathbf{x}$ relative to $\mathcal{C}$ as follows:

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & -1 & 3 \\ 1 & -3 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -4 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ to $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ is given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} =5 \mathbf{c}_1+12\mathbf{c}_2.$

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} . \]

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}&=P^{-1}_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 4 & 3 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{1 \cdot 3 - 1 \cdot 4}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -4 & 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 5 \mathbf{c}_1+12\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain

\[ [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 1 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 12 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ to $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ is given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} = 3\mathbf{c}_1-3\mathbf{c}_2.$

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} . \]

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}&=P^{-1}_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -5 \\ -1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{2\cdot 3-(-1)\cdot (-5)}\begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 3\mathbf{c}_1-3\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain \[ [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}=\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ to $\mathcal{C} = \{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$ is given below. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}$ given that $\mathbf{x} =4\mathbf{c}_1+6\mathbf{c}_2.$

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} . \]

First, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}&=P^{-1}_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 7 \\ 3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}^{-1} \\[5pt] &=\dfrac{1}{4 \cdot 6 - 7 \cdot 3}\begin{bmatrix} 6& -7 \\- 3 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & -\dfrac73 \\ -1 & \dfrac 4 3 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Notice that since $\mathbf{x} = 4\mathbf{c}_1+6\mathbf{c}_2,$ we obtain

\[ [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \]

The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} . \]

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 8 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 5 & 8 \end{bmatrix} ^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{2 \cdot 8 - 5 \cdot 3 }\begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 & -3 \\ -5 & 2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} . \]

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 7 & 3 \\ 3 & 2 \end{bmatrix} ^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{7 \cdot 2 - 3 \cdot 3 }\begin{bmatrix} 2 & -3 \\ -3 & 7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} & -\dfrac{3}{5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} & \dfrac{7}{5} \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} \dfrac{2}{5} & -\dfrac{3}{5} \\ -\dfrac{3}{5} & \dfrac{7}{5} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -7 \\ 18 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 11 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{S}}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
We will use the change-of-coordinates formula in the form

\[ [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} = P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} . \]

First, recall that the change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{S}$ is the matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the standard basis $\mathcal{S}.$ As a result, we have

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Now, we need to find the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}}$ from $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathcal{B}.$ To do that, we compute the inverse of $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}\mathbin{:}$

\[\begin{align*} P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{S}}^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 4 & 1 \\ 11 & 3 \end{bmatrix} ^{-1} \\[5pt] &= \dfrac {1}{4 \cdot 3 - 11 \cdot 1 }\begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}\]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{S}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{S}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -1 \\ -11 & 4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \]

The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{C}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 2 & 4 & 3 & 4 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-1)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 3 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1 +(-3)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & -1 & -8\\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= \dfrac{1}{2}R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & -\dfrac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 & 3 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ is

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -\dfrac{1}{2} & -4 \\ 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &=\begin{bmatrix} -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{C}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 2 & 0 & 4 & 2 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= \dfrac{1}{2}R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 1 & -1 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-4)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -9 & -4 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ is

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -9 & -4 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 1 \\ -9 & -4 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -16 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix}. \]

The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 3 & 4 & -2 & 0 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-3)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -3 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1 +(-1)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 0 & 1 & -2 & -3 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ is \[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 &4\\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4\\ -2 & -3 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -24 \\ 15 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

question.text:
\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \]

The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{C}$ to $\mathcal{B}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{C}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{c}_1$ and $\mathbf{c}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 & \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination:

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 4 & 5 & -3 & -2 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-4)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & 2 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1 +(-1)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 0 & 13 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -11 & -6 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}}$ is

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} = \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{C}\to\mathcal{B}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 13 & 7 \\ -11 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -5 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -9 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

\[ \mathcal{B}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad \mathcal{C}=\bigg\{ \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 6 \end{bmatrix} \bigg\}, \qquad [\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{B}}=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \]

The bases $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ of $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the coordinates of the vector $\mathbf{x}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{B}$ are given above. Find $[\mathbf{x}]_{\mathcal{C}}.$
question.explanation:
Let's denote the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{C}$ as $\{ \mathbf{b}_1,\mathbf{b}_2 \}$ and $\{ \mathbf{c}_1,\mathbf{c}_2 \}$, respectively.

The change-of-coordinates matrix from $\mathcal{B}$ to $\mathcal{C}$ is a matrix whose columns are the vectors of $\mathcal{B}$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$

Hence, we need to find the coordinates of $\mathbf{b}_1$ and $\mathbf{b}_2$ relative to the basis $\mathcal{C}.$ We can do this simultaneously by considering the matrix \[ M = \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \\ \mathbf{c}_1 & \mathbf{c}_2 & \mathbf{b}_1 & \mathbf{b}_2 \\ \vert & \vert & \vert & \vert \end{array} \right]. \]

Now, we simply reduce the left-hand side to reduced row-echelon form using Gaussian elimination

\begin{align*} M &= \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 5 & 6 & 0 & -1 \end{array} \right] & R_2 &:= R_2 +(-5)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 & 1 & -1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -6 \end{array} \right] & R_1 &:= R_1 +(-1)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[ \begin{array}{cc|cc} 1 &0 & -6 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & 5 & -6 \end{array} \right] \end{align*}

Therefore, the change-of-coordinates matrix $P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}}$ is

\[ P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} = \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 7 \\ 5 & -6 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Finally, we compute $[\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}}\mathbin{:}$

\begin{align*} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{C}} &= P_{\small\mathcal{B}\to\mathcal{C}} [\,\mathbf{x}\,]_{\mathcal{B}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -6 & 7 \\ 5 & -6 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}
